summary:
FLARE is an AI-powered research intelligence platform that transforms NASA’s complex microgravity combustion data into accessible, actionable insights for space fire safety.

Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, FLARE addresses the difficulty of discovering, comparing, and interpreting experimental results from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database.

Our platform combines an interactive research dashboard, intelligent experiment search, cross-study comparisons, and an evidence-grounded AI agent. Users can explore how oxygen concentration, gravity, pressure, airflow, and fuel materials influence combustion behavior. An interactive flame simulation laboratory helps visualize different environmental scenarios, while research gap analysis identifies areas requiring further investigation.

Unlike traditional research databases, FLARE connects scientific findings with their original sources, highlights experimental limitations, and helps researchers distinguish measured evidence from theoretical predictions.

By turning fragmented research into understandable scientific insights, FLARE supports better-informed fire safety research, spacecraft design, and future human exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond.
details:
FLARE (Fire Laboratory for Analysis, Research & Exploration) is a web-based platform we built for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to address the "Flame in Freefall" challenge.

NASA has spent years studying how fire behaves in microgravity, but finding and comparing results from its Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database can be difficult. We wanted to make that research easier to explore and more useful for improving fire safety in space.

With FLARE, users can search NASA combustion experiments, compare results, and explore how gravity, oxygen, pressure, and airflow affect fire behavior. But we wanted to go further than building another research dashboard.

One of the biggest parts of our project is the agentic AI research assistant. We connected NVIDIA's Nemotron model through its API and developed a system that allows the assistant to use tools within our application. Instead of only answering questions, it can help users work through several stages of a research task, from finding relevant experiments and comparing evidence to setting up simulations and developing research hypotheses.

We're also exploring KrillClaw to extend the assistant's ability to coordinate longer, multi-step research workflows. For example, a user could ask FLARE to investigate how oxygen levels affect flame spread in spacecraft materials. The assistant could identify relevant NASA experiments, compare their conditions, prepare a simulation, and help the user identify unanswered questions. Our aim is to let users focus on the research problem rather than manually switching between different tools.

Another feature we're excited about is the interactive combustion simulator, where users can explore conditions representing the ISS, Moon, and Mars. It uses simplified theoretical models rather than validated fire predictions, but it provides a hands-on way to understand how environmental conditions influence combustion. We also built a research gap tool that highlights areas where experimental evidence is limited.

We developed FLARE using Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Supabase, and scientific visualization libraries. One of our main challenges was making complex research understandable without losing accuracy. We also had to consider how to keep AI-generated explanations connected to reliable sources, which is why we included citation checks and experimental limitations.

We want to measure FLARE's usefulness by comparing how long users take to find and analyze NASA experiments with and without our platform. We also plan to evaluate the accuracy of experiment comparisons and how consistently the assistant supports its answers with valid scientific citations.

In practice, FLARE could help engineers find relevant evidence when evaluating spacecraft materials, researchers identify experiments worth conducting for lunar and Martian habitats, and students explore combustion science more easily.

What makes FLARE different is that it brings these tasks together. Users can start with a research question and work toward a source-backed explanation, a comparison, a theoretical simulation, or a new research hypothesis without having to navigate several disconnected platforms.

FLARE isn't meant to replace physical experiments or make spacecraft safety decisions on its own. We built it to help people make better use of the research NASA has already collected.

As humans prepare to spend more time on the Moon, Mars, and beyond, understanding fire in unfamiliar environments will become increasingly important. We hope FLARE can help turn NASA's existing research into better research questions, more informed engineering decisions, and ultimately, safer environments for astronauts.
